questions.explanation: A Stack follows **LIFO** (Last In, First Out) — the last element pushed is the first to be popped. **LILO** (Last In, Last Out) is another way to express the same concept. FIFO describes a Queue, not a Stack.

questions.q: `PushBack(Key)` in a single linked list **without a tail** is …
questions.explanation: Without a tail pointer, you must traverse the entire list to reach the last node before appending. This traversal visits every node, giving a time complexity of $O(n)$.

questions.q: ………… is a contiguous area of memory consisting of equal-size elements.
questions.explanation: An **Array** stores elements in contiguous memory locations, and each element occupies the same fixed size. This is what allows $O(1)$ random access via index arithmetic.

questions.q: What is the access time required to retrieve the element located at position $(5, 9)$ in a **7-row and 12-column** array?
questions.explanation:
For row-major order, the formula is:
$$\text{addr} = \text{arr\_addr} + \text{elem\_size} \times ((\text{row} - 1) \times \text{num\_cols} + (\text{col} - 1))$$
Substituting row $= 5$, col $= 9$, num_cols $= 12$:
$$= \text{arr\_addr} + \text{elem\_size} \times ((5-1) \times 12 + (9-1))$$

questions.q: The complexity of adding **two elements** to the end of an array is …
questions.explanation: Adding a fixed number of elements (here, 2) to the end of an array with available capacity is a constant-time operation. $O(2)$ simplifies to $O(1)$ in Big-O notation since constants are dropped.

questions.q: In the Queue implementation with an array, the Queue is **empty** when …
questions.explanation: In a circular array-based Queue, `read` is the index of the next element to dequeue and `write` is where the next element will be enqueued. When `read = write`, there are no elements between them — the Queue is **empty**.

questions.q: To **return** the most recently-added key in a stack, we use the ………… function.
questions.explanation: `KeyTop()` (also known as `Top()` or `Peek()`) returns the key of the top element **without removing it**. `Pop()` removes the top element, `Push(key)` adds one, and `KeyPop()` is not a standard operation.

An **Array** is the data structure defined by indexing via contiguous integers (e.g., indices 0, 1, 2, …, n−1), enabling direct $O(1)$ access. Stacks and Queues are abstract data types that don't inherently require integer indexing.

questions.q: Enqueue is implemented using the ………… function.
questions.explanation: A Queue follows FIFO. **Enqueue** adds an element to the **back/tail** of the queue, which corresponds to `PushBack(Key)` in a linked list implementation.

questions.q: The drawback of dynamic arrays is that some space is wasted.
questions.explanation: **True.** Dynamic arrays (e.g., `std::vector`) over-allocate capacity to amortize the cost of resizing. For example, when the array doubles in size, up to half of the allocated memory may be unused at any given time — this is the space trade-off.

questions.q:
The correct order for the following lines in the `PushBack(key)` function is …

| Label | Line |
|---|---|
| a | `node.next ← nil` |
| b | `node.key ← key` |
| c | `node.next ← head` |
| d | `head ← tail ← node` |
| e | `if tail = nil:` |
| f | `Else:` |
| g | `tail.next ← node` |
| h | `node ← new node` |
| i | `tail ← node` |
questions.explanation:
The correct order is **h → b → a → e → d → f → g → i**:
1. `h`: Allocate a new node
2. `b`: Set its key
3. `a`: Set `node.next ← nil` (it will be the last node)
4. `e`: Check if the list is empty (`tail = nil`)
5. `d`: If empty, both `head` and `tail` point to the new node
6. `f`: Else (list is not empty)
7. `g`: Link current tail to the new node
8. `i`: Update `tail` to the new node

Note: Options **a** and **d** are identical — the answer is **a** (index 0).
options: h, b, a, e, d, f, g, i
h, b, c, e, d, f, g, i
h, b, a, e, d, f, i, g
h, b, a, e, d, f, g, i

questions.q: Which of the following does **NOT** allow heterogeneous data elements?
questions.explanation: An **Array** stores elements of a single, fixed data type in contiguous memory — it does **not** allow heterogeneous (mixed-type) data. Stacks, Queues, and Linked Lists are abstract structures that can be implemented to hold any type, including heterogeneous data.

questions.q: Access time for the **10th element** in a single-dimensional Array is equal to …
questions.explanation:
The general formula for 1D array element access is:
$$\text{addr}(i) = \text{arr\_addr} + \text{elem\_size} \times (i - \text{first\_index})$$
For the 10th element ($i = 10$):
$$= \text{arr\_addr} + \text{elem\_size} \times (10 - \text{first\_index})$$
Option b uses $i$ (a variable) instead of the specific value 10, option c incorrectly multiplies the base address, and option d omits `elem_size`.
